chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil ibn Dirraj from Salama ibn Muhraz said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Indeed, an Armani man died and bequeathed to me.' He said, 'And what is the Armani?' I said, 'A Nabati from the Nabati of the mountains. He died and bequeathed to me his estate and left a daughter.' He said to me, 'Give her half.'

He said, 'So I informed Zurarah of that, and he said to me, 'Be careful (of me), for the wealth is entirely hers.' He said, 'So I entered upon him later and said, 'May Allah improve you, our companions claimed that you were cautious (of me).' He said, 'No, by Allah, I was not cautious of you, but I was sparing you (from error). Did anyone know of that?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Then give her what remains.'

key_terms.أَرْمَانِيٌّ: Armani (a specific ethnic or religious group, often Syriac/Christian)
key_terms.نَبَطِيٌّ: Nabati (from the Nabataeans, often used for rural or mountain dwellers)

ai.seo_question: What is the inheritance ruling for a daughter when her non-Muslim father bequeaths his estate to a Muslim?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *ittiba'* (following the apparent ruling) versus *ihtiyat* (caution), where Imam al-Sadiq initially advised giving the daughter half to avoid potential dispute with other claimants, but Zurarah’s precise knowledge of the specific bequest (*wasiyya*) led to the full estate being awarded to her. It highlights the scholarly nuance between general inheritance rules and specific testamentary dispositions, emphasizing that the Imam’s guidance was tailored to the narrator’s level of certainty rather than a change in legal principle. This reflects the Shia emphasis on contextual application of law, where the Imam’s wisdom (*hikma*) guides the companion to the most accurate outcome based on available information.
